title: CPU-side bottlenecks: tokenization, request parsing, thread pools (action plan)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures findings from recent CPU-side profiling runs focused on three recurring hotspots in the serving runtime: tokenization, request parsing/validation, and thread-pool contention / Python overhead. It consolidates microbenchmarks, flamegraph observations, hypotheses about root causes, and an actionable remediation plan with owners and expected impact.

Context and motivation:
- Multiple customer incidents and internal perf tests showed elevated p95/p99 tail latencies on small-to-medium requests even when GPU utilization was low.
- Flamegraphs sampled on production-like load point to significant CPU time spent outside the GPU pipeline: tokenization, JSON parsing & validation, and Python threading/serialization overhead.
- Goal: reduce p95/p99 by 20-40% for short prompt workloads (<= 128 tokens) by moving CPU work off the critical path or speeding it up.

Profiling methodology and artifacts collected:
- Workload: 1000 concurrent requests across 4 replicas, prompt length distribution: 50% short (<=64 tokens), 40% medium (65-256), 10% long (>256).
- Tools used: py-spy (sampling), pyinstrument, linux perf (cycles), flamegraph.pl, perf top, orjson bench, and a custom harness (bench/serve_bench.py) that mimics real client behaviour.
- Baseline numbers (serving node with 16 CPU cores, 1x A100):
  - median latency (end-to-end): 80 ms
  - p95 latency: 190 ms
  - p99 latency: 420 ms
  - CPU utilization: 45-70% depending on burst
- Representative profiling snapshot (short prompts, p99 tail):
  - tokenization (Python tokenizer pipeline): ~30-40% CPU samples
  - request parsing + pydantic validation: ~12-18% CPU samples
  - serialization / JSON encode (or builtins): ~8-12%
  - threadpool context switching / GIL contention: ~10% (higher under increased concurrency)
  - idle / scheduler: remainder

Key findings and hypotheses:
1) Tokenization is a major CPU consumer for short prompts
   - The current tokenizer implementation is a Python wrapper around a slower C extension in one path and a pure-Python fallback path in some branches. Under certain prompt shapes we hit the fallback path which is ~3x slower.
   - Flamegraphs show heavy time spent in token normalization, whitespace splitting, and Python-level regex ops in the fallback code.
   - Microbenchmarks: replacing fallback with the Rust-based HF Tokenizers reduces tokenization CPU by ~3.5x and median tokenization latency from 18ms -> 5ms for short prompts.

2) Request parsing and validation (JSON -> Pydantic models) is non-trivial
   - We observed ~12-18% of CPU spent in Pydantic model validation for route handlers that eagerly validate the full request payload.
   - Large nested metadata objects and repeated field coercions (dates, enums) amplify cost.
   - Using orjson for raw JSON parse yields ~2.5x faster deserialization compared to Python's json. However converting to Pydantic still dominates unless we adopt .construct() paths or typed memoryviews for hot fields.

3) Thread pool configuration + Python overhead causes tail latency
   - Our runtime offloads tokenization and other CPU-bound work to a ThreadPoolExecutor shared with network handling threads. Under high concurrency threads contend, causing increased context switching and GIL thrash.
   - Observed blocking on queue waits and long-lived threads recycling.
   - Default threadpool size was heuristically set to 2 * cpu_count; this causes over-subscription when combined with async event loop and blocking IO.

4) Allocation churn and temporary objects (short-lived) increase GC pauses
   - Hot paths allocate many small Python objects (str slices, token objects) which increase GC frequency and stray into stop-the-world pauses at p99.

Remediation options (ranked by expected impact / complexity):
A) High impact, moderate effort: Replace Python fallback tokenizer with HF-Rust tokenizer (fast-tokenizers) and expose a C-extension or small Rust shim.
   - Expected impact: tokenization CPU drop 3-4x, p95/p99 latency reduction 15-25% for short prompts.
   - Risks: additional binary deps in Private deployments; need packaging for on-prem.
   - Owner: Aisha Kapoor. ETA: 3 weeks for PoC, 6-8 weeks for rollout + packaging.

B) Medium impact, low effort: switch JSON load/dump to orjson + use Pydantic v1 optimizations (or move to pydantic-core for v2 where available). Defer full model validation to async background when possible.
   - Expected impact: 10-15% CPU reduction on parsing-heavy routes.
   - Owner: Maya Chen. ETA: 1 week to flip in staging, 2-3 weeks to validate.

C) Medium impact, medium effort: rework request handling to parse minimally on hot path (extract only required fields) and validate noncritical fields asynchronously or lazily.
   - Pattern: use a lightweight struct (or TypedDict) created via orjson.loads and only validate when fields are used.
   - Owner: Jonah Rivera. ETA: 3-4 weeks.

D) Medium impact, medium effort: move CPU-bound tasks to isolated worker processes (ProcessPoolExecutor) or a small Rust microservice to avoid GIL contention. Use shared memory / msgpack for zero-copy where possible.
   - Expected impact: reduces GIL contention and allows true parallelism, but increases IPC costs.
   - Owner: Priya Nair. ETA: 4-6 weeks for pilot.

E) Low-to-medium impact, low effort: tune ThreadPoolExecutor size and ensure heavy CPU tasks run in a dedicated pool separate from IO threadpool. Add bounded queues and backpressure so CPU tasks don't pile up.
   - Changes: default pool size -> cpu_count (instead of 2*), create dedicated pool for tokenization of size cpu_count-1, set max queue length per worker and return 429/Retry-After when overloaded.
   - Expected impact: improves tail stability and reduces p99 under load spikes.
   - Owner: Samir Patel. ETA: 1 week for experiments, 2 weeks for rollout.

F) Low effort: enable orjson for both parsing and response encoding, reuse bytearray buffers for repeated serializations, and prefer memoryview for binary data to avoid copies.
   - Owner: Maya Chen. ETA: 3 days.

G) Instrumentation: add lightweight per-request timing breakdowns (tokenize_ms, parse_ms, queue_wait_ms, handler_ms) to logs and metrics so we can observe changes in prod. Also ship flamegraphs from canary nodes nightly for the first 2 weeks after rollout.
   - Owner: Observability (assigned: Erik Holt). ETA: 2 weeks.

Microbenchmarks and commands used:
- Tokenizer microbench: bench/tokenizer_bench.py
  - python -m pyinstrument bench/tokenizer_bench.py --samples 1000
  - Results: Python fallback median 18ms/tokenize for 64-byte prompts; HF Tokenizers (Rust) median 5ms.
- JSON parsing: bench/json_parse_bench.py using orjson vs json
  - orjson.loads: ~0.35ms per small payload, json.loads: ~0.9ms.
- Profile capture: py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python bench/serve_bench.py --concurrency 100 --duration 300
- Perf for cycles: sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g --pid <pid> -- sleep 60; perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf.svg

Instrumentation to add before rollout:
- Request-level fields in metrics: tokenize_ms, parse_ms, validate_ms, serialization_ms, queue_wait_ms.
- Count of requests hitting fallback tokenizer path.
- Threadpool queue length histogram + worker busy ratio.
- GC pause duration histograms (via tracemalloc/gc).

Risk / compatibility notes:
- Rust tokenizer binary must be packaged for Private deployments (vendor shim or prebuilt wheels). Work with release-engineering to ensure hermetic builds.
- Using ProcessPoolExecutor increases memory usage; measure memory footprint on Dedicated workloads.
- Pydantic v2 migration has compatibility changes; prefer a migration window with feature flags.

Decision / next steps (action items):
1) Flip orjson for parsing in staging and run 48h smoke: Owner Maya Chen. Due: 2024-10-18.
2) Implement threadpool tuning experiment (dedicated pool for tokenizers, queue bounds): Owner Samir Patel. Due: 2024-10-20.
   - Measure p95/p99 and CPU utilization against baseline.
3) PoC HF-Rust tokenizer integration with a small shim, include a test packaging build for on-prem: Owner Aisha Kapoor. Due: 2024-11-01.
4) Add per-request timing metrics and nightly flamegraph capture on canaries: Owner Observability. Due: 2024-10-25.
5) Run a follow-up load test 2 weeks after tokenization rollout to measure regression/impact: Owner Jonah Rivera. Due: 2024-11-15.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Is the cost of adding a native dependency acceptable for customers who run Private on very locked-down infra? (sales/legal ask)
- Should we default to process-based tokenization on Dedicated to avoid GIL interference rather than changing threadpools?
- Do we want an opt-in feature flag for pre-tokenization caching for common prompts (privacy implications)?

Notes from related artifacts / previous work:
- Existing ticket JIRA-1234 tracked a similar incident in Aug 2024; that investigation recommended orjson but lacked tokenizer PoC.
- GH PR rti-tokenizer-opt/pull/78 contains initial Rust shim code and benchmark scripts (bench/tokenizer_bench.py).

Appendix: quick checklist for rolling changes
- [ ] Add metrics + logs for per-request breakdown to staging.
- [ ] Run orjson flip and validate schema compatibility with current clients.
- [ ] Deploy threadpool tuning (feature flag) and run A/B on canaries.
- [ ] Merge HF-Rust tokenizer PoC behind feature flag; run packaging tests for Private.
- [ ] If PoC validated, plan gradual rollout: 10% -> 50% -> 100% with nightly flamegraphs.

Contact / follow-ups:
- Slack: #eng-serving-runtime (tag: @samir)
- Pager: on-call SRE for serving runtime during rollout windows

If reviewers agree with the plan I propose we start with the low-effort wins (orjson, threadpool tune) this week, then run tokenizer PoC in parallel.

-- Samir Patel
